intro.text:
In the Old Quarter of Hanoi, there is an alley named after a village in Thái Bình: Phất Lộc.

According to sources on local history, residents who left their home village to make a living in Thăng Long brought the old village name with them to name their new home.

Over many generations, Phất Lộc became a place to live and trade. The Tiên Hạ Temple in the alley is associated with the noted official Nguyễn Trung Ngạn of the Trần dynasty, while the bún đậu stalls and simple eateries carry on the story of the people's livelihoods.

Phất Lộc is therefore more than the name of an alley. It is the mark of people who carried the memory of their homeland to build a new life in the heart of Thăng Long, Hanoi.

alleyStory.title: Phất Lộc Alley
paragraphs: Contrary to the common interpretation that Phất Lộc means prosperity and good fortune, the alley's name is actually linked to Phất Lộc village in the former Thái Bình Province.

According to the Vietnam National Authority of Tourism (2024), people who came from Phất Lộc village to settle and make a living in Thăng Long brought the village name with them for their new home. One research source refers to migration from the seventeenth century, while a local account recorded by VietnamPlus (2024b) mentions a Bùi-surname scholar who came to Thăng Long in 1717. The alley's formation should therefore not be assigned a single date.

Phất Lộc Alley has many narrow branches that meet near Tiên Hạ Temple, which honors Nguyễn Trung Ngạn, a notable official of the Trần dynasty. The temple also has a restoration stele written by Nguyễn Siêu in 1886 (Sài Gòn Giải Phóng, 2006).

According to Ngọc Nhi (2018), Phất Lộc was once home to many working families, including rickshaw drivers, small business owners, and street vendors. As tourism in the Old Quarter grew, commerce and services in the alley gradually changed. Bún đậu mắm tôm became a signature dish associated with the alley.
Distinctive character: The name holds memories of a homeland, a migrant community, a place of worship, and the livelihoods of local families.

eat.name: Bún đậu Hương
eat.dishes: Bún đậu mắm tôm, fried tofu, chả cốm, and side dishes.

eat.name: Bún riêu shops in Phất Lộc Alley
eat.dishes: Crab noodle soup, snail noodle soup, and other traditional noodle dishes.
eat.note: Varies by shop; no common schedule has been established.

eat.name: Bún đậu Trung Hương
eat.address: Previously listed address: 49 Phất Lộc Alley
eat.dishes: Associated with the story of Ms. Hương's family's business growing from a street-vending basket.

visit.name: Tiên Hạ Temple
notes: A religious site associated with Nguyễn Trung Ngạn, an official who played an important role in the history of Thăng Long under the Trần dynasty.
The site has architectural traces and records of a nineteenth-century restoration.
Public sources list house numbers 46 or 48; the exact address has not been confirmed. Confirm visiting hours before going (Sài Gòn Giải Phóng, 2006).

visit.name: Branches of Phất Lộc Alley
notes: Observe the narrow alley layout, its connections to other streets, and the mix of homes and businesses.
This area can support exploration of Old Quarter housing and community livelihoods.
Observe from public paths only; do not enter private homes or residential areas without permission (Ngọc Nhi, 2018).

route: Hear the story of the migrant community
Explore bún đậu and bún riêu
caveats: Ngọc Nhi's 2018 interview is a useful source for the story of how the Trung Hương bún đậu family's livelihood developed. The listing does not establish that the shop still operates at the same address or hours shown in older directories.
